title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-324-080-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-324-080-001
Issues
1. Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence
that she suffered a compensable right shoulder injury during the course and scope of
employment with Employer on July 19, 2025.
2. Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that
she is entitled to receive reasonable and necessary medical benefits that are causally
related to her July 19, 2025 right shoulder injury.
Procedural Matter
On May 28, 2026 Claimant filed the following two motions: (1) an Opposed
Motion for Extension of Time to File Proposed Findings of Fact; and (2) an Opposed
Motion to Reopen the Evidentiary Record. The motions are predicated on Claimant’s
May 19, 2026 diagnostic imaging including a Cervical Spine MRI and a Brachial Plexus
MRI. Claimant asserts the preceding reports contain critical, objective anatomical
findings that were not available at the time of the May 14, 2026 hearing. She promptly
provided the reports to Respondents’ counsel upon receipt on May 26, 2026. Claimant
contends that there is good cause for the reopening of the record to admit the reports
because their consideration “is necessary to ensure a complete medical record and to
prevent manifest injustice, as the findings directly correlate to the Claimant’s
documented impairment and determination of medical benefits.”
Despite Claimant’s arguments, she has failed to demonstrate good cause to
reopen the evidentiary record or extend the due date for filing position statements. An
ALJ has broad discretion over the conduct of hearings, including the timing and
admission of evidence. Notably, under §8-43-207(1)(i) C.R.S., an ALJ may grant
reasonable extensions of time for the taking of any action contained in the article for
good cause shown. Factors including timeliness, diligence, prejudice to opposing

parties, and the probative value of the additional evidence are significant when
determining whether good cause exists.
The critical inquiry in the present matter is whether Claimant’s work activities on
July 19, 2025 caused a right shoulder injury. The condition of Claimant’s right shoulder
is not the pivotal inquiry in determining compensability. Additional diagnostic testing will
not provide material or probative information regarding the cause of Claimant’s right
shoulder condition. Moreover, Claimant has not explained why the MRI testing could not
have been reasonably performed or the results obtained prior to the May 17, 2026
hearing in this matter. Finally, Respondents did not have an opportunity to address the
MRI findings on the date of the hearing. Accordingly, Claimant’s request to reopen the
evidentiary record and extend the due date for filing position statements is denied. The
evidence is closed and position statements were due by May 28, 2026.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant is a 40-year-old Massage Therapist who alleges an injury to her
right shoulder while performing a couple’s massage on July 19, 2025. She detailed that
she went to work on July 19, 2025 and her last client of the day was a two-hour couple’s
massage. Claimant conducted a deep tissue massage on the male. She finished the
massage and performed closing duties, including folding laundry and preparing the
massage room for the next day.
2. Claimant went home, rested, showered and prepared for bed. She laid
down in bed on her right side. Claimant lifted her arm above her head and across her
body. She noticed a sharp pain in the anterior aspect of her right shoulder. Claimant
attributed her pain to simply overworking after seven or eight hours of full-scheduled
hands-on massages.
3. Claimant went to work on the following day of July 20, 2025. She
performed a deep tissue massage and completed her shift. She did not notice any
additional pain after work on July 20, 2025.
4. Claimant’s last day working for Employer was July 20, 2026. Although she
was scheduled for two additional shifts, she called out from work due to illness.
Claimant had emailed Employer on either July 16 or 17, 2025 and informed them that

she was resigning as of July 26, 2025. She had accepted another position at Wellness
Spa RX as a massage therapist with a start date of August 1, 2025.
5. Claimant acknowledged she did not report her injury to Employer’s
General Manager Sabrina Salazar or the lead therapist on either July 19, 2025 or July
20, 2025 because she did not realize she had an issue to report.
6. Claimant worked at two other massage facilities before she started
developing pain in her right shoulder in October 2025. She did not seek treatment for
her right shoulder until November 19, 2025.
7. On November 20, 2025 Claimant reported her right shoulder injury to Ms.
Salazar. Ms. Salazar noted that at no time did the other masseuse, , who
was in the couple’s massage with Claimant on the alleged date of injury, report that
Claimant suffered an injury.
8. On April 15, 2026 Claimant underwent an Independent Medical
Examination (IME) with Douglas C. Scott, M.D. Dr. Scott prepared a report and testified
at the hearing in this matter. He considered Claimant’s medical history and mechanism
of injury. Claimant told Dr. Scott that during the July 19, 2025 massage she did not feel
pain, popping or experience a specific injury to her right shoulder. Claimant detailed that
she did not feel symptoms during any of the massages on July 19, 2025. There was no
specific injurious event.
9. Claimant acknowledged the first time she felt pain was when she was at
home, lying in bed, moving her arm across her body. She specifically experienced a
sharp pain on the front side of her right shoulder. Claimant was able to complete the
deep tissue massage the following day with no pain or popping in her shoulder. She
recounted that during her work with a subsequent Employer, Wellness Spa Rx, she
started to gradually feel soreness in the anterior right shoulder without a specific injury
or event.
10. Dr. Scott noted that on January 21, 2026 Claimant underwent an MRI of
the right upper extremity. He explained that the imaging revealed findings of partial
subscapularis tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis. Dr. Scott remarked
the diagnosis was unrelated to the alleged work injury. He commented that the
radiologist’s reading of the MRI scan “suggests that the findings of partial subscapularis

tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis were chronic and possibly all of
these findings pre-existed 7/19/2025.” Dr. Scott also explained that, if Claimant suffered
a rotator cuff tear on July 19, 2025, she would not have been able to perform massages
the following day without reported pain or dysfunction.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured
workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-
40-102(1), C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of
proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S.
A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering
all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197
Colo. 306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004).
The facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either
the rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A
Workers' Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of
the issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might
lead to a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings
as unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness’ testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
4. For a claim to be compensable under the Act, a claimant has the burden of
proving that he suffered a disability that was proximately caused by an injury arising out
of and within the course and scope of employment. §8-41-301(1)(c) C.R.S.; In re

Swanson, W.C. No. 4-589-645 (ICAO, Sept. 13, 2006). Proof of causation is a threshold
requirement that an injured employee must establish by a preponderance of the evidence
before any compensation is awarded. Faulkner v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 12 P.3d 844,
846 (Colo. App. 2000); Singleton v. Kenya Corp., 961 P.2d 571, 574 (Colo. App. 1998).
The question of causation is generally one of fact for determination by the Judge.
Faulkner, 12 P.3d at 846.
5. A pre-existing condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim
if the employment aggravates, accelerates or combines with the pre-existing condition to
produce a need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d
999, 1001 (Colo. App. 2004). A compensable injury is one that causes disability or the
need for medical treatment. City of Boulder v. Payne, 162 Colo. 345, 426 P.2d 194 (1967);
Mailand v. PSC Indus. Outsourcing LP, W.C. No. 4-898-391-01, (ICAO, Aug. 25, 2014).
6. Section 8-41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. requires that an injury be “proximately
caused by an injury or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of the
employee’s employment.” Thus, the claimant is required to prove a direct causal
relationship between the injury and the disability and need for treatment. However, the
industrial injury need not be the sole cause of the disability if the injury is a significant,
direct, and consequential factor in the disability. See Subsequent Injury Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 131 P.3d 1224 (Colo. App. 2006); Joslins Dry Goods Co. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 21 P.3d 866 (Colo. App. 2001).
7. The mere fact a claimant experiences symptoms while performing work
does not require the inference that there has been an aggravation or acceleration of a
pre-existing condition. See Cotts v. Exempla, Inc., W.C. No. 4-606-563 (ICAO, Aug. 18,
2005). Rather, the symptoms could represent the “logical and recurrent consequence” of
the pre-existing condition. See F.R. Orr Construction v. Rinta, 717 P.2d 965 (Colo. App.
1985); Chasteen v. King Soopers, Inc., W.C. No. 4-445-608 (ICAO, Apr. 10, 2008). As
explained in Scully v. Hooters of Colorado Springs, W.C. No. 4-745-712 (ICAO, Oct. 27,
2008), simply because a claimant’s symptoms arise after the performance of a job
function does not necessarily create a causal relationship based on temporal proximity.
The panel in Scully noted that “correlation is not causation,” and merely because a

coincidental correlation exists between the claimant’s work and symptoms does not mean
there is a causal connection between the claimant’s injury and work activities.
8. The provision of medical care based on a claimant’s report of symptoms
does not establish an injury but only demonstrates that the claimant claimed an injury.
Washburn v. City Market, W.C. No. 5-109-470 (ICAO, June 3, 2020). Moreover, a referral
for medical care may be made so that the respondent would not forfeit its right to select
the medical providers if the claim is later deemed compensable. Id. Although a physician
may provide diagnostic testing, treatment, and work restrictions based on a claimant’s
reported symptoms, there is no mandate that the claimant suffered a compensable injury.
Fay v. East Penn Manufacturing Co., Inc., W.C. No. 5-108-430-001 (ICAO, Apr. 24,
2020); see Snyder v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 942 P.2d 1337, 1339 (Colo. App. 1997)
(“right to workers' compensation benefits, including medical payments, arises only when
an injured employee initially establishes, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the
need for medical treatment was proximately caused by an injury arising out of and in the
course of the employment”). While scientific evidence is not dispositive of compensability,
the ALJ may consider and rely on medical opinions regarding the lack of a scientific theory
supporting compensability. Savio House v. Dennis, 665 P.2d 141 (Colo. App. 1983);
Washburn v. City Market, W.C. No. 5-109-470 (ICAO, June 3, 2020).
9. Claimant has failed to establish by a preponderance of the evidence that
she suffered a compensable right shoulder injury during the course and scope of her
employment with Employer on July 19, 2025. Claimant acknowledged she did not feel
pain or symptoms while performing the deep tissue massage on the date of injury.
However, she mentioned a sharp pain at home when she moved her arm above her head
and across her body while lying in bed. Furthermore, Claimant acknowledged she felt no
pain the following day while completing her work duties with Employer including a deep
tissue massage. Notably, she did not feel symptoms in her right shoulder until October
2025 and did not seek treatment until November 19, 2025.
10. Dr. Scott commented that on January 21, 2026 Claimant underwent an MRI
of the right upper extremity. He persuasively explained that the imaging revealed findings
of partial subscapularis tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis. Dr. Scott
remarked the diagnosis was unrelated to the alleged work injury. He commented that the

radiologist’s reading of the MRI scan “suggests that the findings of partial subscapularis
tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis were chronic and possibly all of
these findings pre-existed 7/19/2025.” Furthermore, if Claimant suffered a rotator cuff tear
on July 19, 2025, she would not have been able to perform massages the following day
without reported pain or dysfunction.
11. Despite Claimant’s contention that her work activities caused her right
shoulder injury, the weight of the persuasive medical evidence reflects that she has failed
to demonstrate a causal connection to her employment. Initially, Claimant acknowledged
she felt no pain on July 20, 2025 while completing her work duties with Employer including
a deep tissue massage. Notably, although a temporal delay in the development of
symptoms and reporting is not dispositive of compensability, Claimant did not experience
significant right shoulder symptoms until October 2025 and did not seek treatment until
November 19, 2025. Finally, the January 21, 2026 right upper extremity MRI revealed
chronic findings. The preceding factors suggest that it is speculative to attribute her right
shoulder symptoms to her July 19, 2025 work activities. Accordingly, Claimant’s request
for Workers’ Compensation benefits is denied and dismissed.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant’s request for Workers’ Compensation benefits is denied and
dismissed.
2. Any issues not resolved in this Order are reserved for future
determination.
If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review
the order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the Judge; and (2) That
you mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. For

statutory reference, see section 8-43-301(2), C.R.S. For further information regarding
procedures to follow when filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may
access a petition to review form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
Dated: June 3, 2026 _

Administrative Law Judge
